name: Artane-Whitehall
text: Press coverage of the Artane-Whitehall LEA (Artane, Whitehall, Beaumont, Killester) shows a handful of serious but isolated incidents rather than an ongoing crime pattern. The most significant was a fatal one-punch assault on Larkhill Road, Whitehall, Dublin 9, in the early hours of 30 July 2023: a man was struck outside a taxi during a row over the car door and died two days later; a suspect was charged with manslaughter, with the case sent forward for trial through late 2024. Separately, an armed carjacking occurred in Artane on 4 May 2022, in which a motorist was threatened at gunpoint ('give me the car or I will blow your head off') and with a knife; one participant, a juvenile at the time, was convicted in February 2026, with sentencing pending. More recently, gardai confirmed a fatal incident at a residential address on Brookwood Heights, Artane, in the early hours of 16 May 2026, in which a man in his 30s died and a man in his 60s was arrested and detained — details suggest a contained, likely domestic-type incident rather than street crime, with the Garda investigation still active at time of writing. No evidence was found of the area being a recognised 'no-go' zone, of organised gang turf conflict, or of frequent daytime muggings, assaults on tourists, or repeated public-order disorder specific to Artane, Whitehall, Beaumont or Killester (unlike nearby Coolock, which saw distinct asylum-accommodation protest violence in mid-2024, but which falls outside this LEA). Daytime searches turned up no particular safety concerns — shops, parks, DART stations and residential streets show no reported pattern of incidents. Night-time carries modestly more caution given the documented fatal assault, carjacking and fatal domestic incident, all clustered around late-night/early-morning hours, though these read as isolated serious events years apart rather than a chronic hotspot.

name: Ballyfermot-Drimnagh
text: Press coverage from 2022-2026 shows this LEA has a well-documented, repeated pattern of serious gun and gang crime concentrated in Drimnagh and the Cherry Orchard part of Ballyfermot, alongside lower-level anti-social behaviour elsewhere. The most significant recent event was the fatal shooting of 20-year-old Josh Itseli in Drimnagh on 6 May 2024, in which gunmen in a passing car opened fire before crashing; the Irish Times described 'gunfire, crashed cars, a pipe bomb and a killing' during the chaotic aftermath, with Gardai voicing concern over a 'minor gang's' access to high-powered weapons. Arrests followed in 2025 but suspects were released without charge (RTE, TheJournal.ie, May 2025). Drimnagh and neighbouring Crumlin are also historically associated with the long-running Crumlin-Drimnagh drug feud, which produced numerous gangland killings in the 2000s and is still referenced in ongoing crime reporting. Cherry Orchard, within Ballyfermot, saw well-documented multi-night disorder in early 2022, with the Irish Examiner describing 'scenes of mayhem' over 'five nights of disturbances' and residents demanding more Garda resources; two men were separately charged after an assault on Gardai in Ballyfermot in November 2022. An Irish Times feature from November 2022 quoted residents saying 'nobody wants to live here' due to persistent car theft. Bluebell has had isolated serious incidents, including a teenager left in serious condition after an assault (Irish Times, May 2023) and an earlier shooting/attempted murder at a flat complex. Organised crime remains active locally, illustrated by a €2m cannabis seizure at a Ballyfermot business in June 2025. A tragic father-and-son murder-suicide spanning Ballyfermot and Clondalkin was reported in January 2026, though this stemmed from a domestic custody dispute rather than street crime. No comparable pattern of daytime street violence was found, but the frequency and severity of gun crime and gang activity, particularly after dark, support a cautious rating.

name: Ballymun-Finglas
text: This LEA — covering Ballymun, Finglas, and Santry — shows a well-documented, ongoing pattern of gangland violence concentrated in Ballymun and Finglas, with Santry itself returning no notable safety coverage. Finglas has a long-running drugs-related feud: in November 2023, 23-year-old Brandon Ledwidge was shot dead in a gangland attack tied to a drugs gang dispute, with houses subsequently boarded up as the feud escalated (Irish Times). Fatal stabbings followed in June 2024 and again in November 2024, when a man in his 60s (Mark Carroll) died after an assault, though gardai said he was not the intended target (RTE, Irish Times, Irish Examiner). Ballymun has seen an intensifying and very current feud: a house was petrol-bombed with two people hospitalised, a house was left with bullet holes after a shooting, and a bullet was fired into the bedroom of a sleeping three-year-old, alongside a grenade-style explosion that damaged four homes in May 2026 (Crime World, TheJournal.ie). In October 2025 a man in his 30s was seriously injured in a broad-daylight attack in Ballymun (TheJournal.ie). Most alarmingly, in April 2026 a child discharged a handgun dropped by a suspect fleeing gardai in Ballymun, prompting local representatives to call it a "crisis" requiring government intervention (RTE, Irish Times, dublinpeople.com, Social Democrats statement). Gardai have responded with repeated raids, drug/weapon seizures, and newly launched high-visibility patrols to disrupt criminal activity. Given the frequency, recency, and severity — multiple shootings, murders, explosives, and firearms reaching a child — this pattern is serious and ongoing rather than isolated, though the violence is largely feud-targeted rather than random street crime affecting casual visitors, and daytime incidents are less frequent than nighttime ones.

name: Cabra-Glasnevin
text: Press research on the Cabra-Glasnevin Local Electoral Area (covering Cabra, Glasnevin, and Phibsborough) found no evidence of a pervasive crime pattern or no-go areas, and one notable dated violent incident. In November 2023, two men were hospitalised with serious injuries after a stabbing at the Cabra House pub on the North Circular Road/Cabra area, following the funeral of a local man (Brandon Ledwidge); both were treated at the Mater Hospital, as reported by TheJournal.ie, RTE, and the Irish Examiner. This appears to have been an isolated, feud/funeral-related incident rather than a random attack on the public. Separately, official crime-ranking analysis (drawing on Garda station data) places the Cabra Garda district 35th of 41 Dublin Metropolitan Region districts by recorded offences in 2025 (977 offences), broadly stable since 2019 — indicating a comparatively low-crime area relative to other parts of Dublin. For Glasnevin, the main documented concern is historical: a 2018 burglary spike (30 burglaries in a three-month period, three aggravated) was raised by a local Oireachtas member and residents' policing forum, partly attributed to the 2015 closure of Whitehall Garda station; more recent (2024) Garda "Crimecall" appeals show isolated burglary investigations in Glasnevin (Dublin 9) but no evidence of a continuing spike in the 2023-2026 window. Phibsborough shows no crime-specific news coverage in this period; local news instead centres on dereliction and vacant/derelict buildings (residents' protest reported by TheJournal.ie, March 2026) and the long-delayed redevelopment of Phibsborough Shopping Centre — quality-of-life and urban-decay issues rather than safety incidents. No evidence was found of gang activity, muggings of pedestrians, or repeated violent incidents affecting residents or visitors in daytime. Given the isolated but serious nighttime stabbing and scattered burglary reports, night safety warrants a mild caution (yellow), while daytime conditions show no particular concern (green) based on available reporting.
sources: Finglas Cabra Local Drug & Alcohol Task Force (finglascabraldtf.ie)

name: Clontarf
text: Clontarf overall remains what its reputation suggests: an affluent, seaside residential area, and no evidence emerged of a broad or worsening crime problem across Clontarf, Marino, Fairview or Killester. Daytime life along the seafront, village and park areas shows no documented safety pattern in local press. However, a small number of specific, dated incidents point to some caution after dark or in the early hours. In September 2026, a woman in her twenties was robbed and assaulted around 5:10am on Alfie Byrne Road, the road linking East Wall to Clontarf, by a female suspect in a red puffer jacket; Gardai (Clontarf station) appealed for witnesses and dashcam footage (TheJournal.ie, Crime World, Dublin People, RTE, all Sept 2026). In October 2025, a man in his 50s was left in serious condition after a serious assault near Annesley Bridge in Fairview Park at around 6pm, prompting a Garda technical examination and a witness/dashcam appeal, with a second arrest reported in follow-up coverage (Irish Times, Garda.ie, Crime World, Oct 2025). Separately, local politics coverage (Dublin People, April 2025) reported that Clontarf Garda station's staffing fell from 64 officers in December 2023 to 53 in December 2024, with Sinn Fein TD Denise Mitchell citing a Dublin-wide 9% year-on-year rise in assault, harassment and murder-threat offences for 2024 and warning of reduced community policing visibility. No specific reports of muggings, gang activity, persistent anti-social behaviour hotspots, or no-go areas were found for Marino or Killester in the 2023-2026 window; older references (a 2015 drug seizure, a historic shooting inquest) are too dated or minor to indicate a current pattern. On balance, Clontarf LEA is a genuinely low-crime, low-concern area by day, with two isolated but real violent incidents in the evening/early-morning hours over roughly a year, combined with documented reductions in local Garda staffing, warranting modest caution rather than any characterization as unsafe at night.

name: Donaghmede
text: Press coverage of the Donaghmede Local Electoral Area (which spans Donaghmede, Kilbarrack, Raheny, Bayside and Sutton/Howth) shows no evidence of a general daytime safety problem: shopping streets, parks and the coastal areas around Bayside, Sutton and Howth turned up no dated 2023-2026 news reports of muggings, assaults or notable daytime crime patterns. The recurring, documented concern in this area instead centers on the DART rail line and its stations after dark and in evenings, particularly around Kilbarrack and Howth Junction/Donaghmede stations. TheJournal.ie, 98fm and JOE.ie reported that in June 2021 ambulance personnel and Gardaí were attacked by a group of youths at Kilbarrack DART station. Separately, a violent disorder incident at Howth Junction station (covered by the Irish Times and Irish Examiner) resulted in multiple teenagers being arrested after a melee in which a girl fell under a DART carriage; the case concluded in court with a suspended sentence for one of the youths involved. More recently, TheJournal.ie reported in January 2025 that a 15-year-old boy was charged over a Dart station attack following what was described as a 'complex investigation.' A November 2025 Dublin People article quoted Dublin Bay North TD Barry Heneghan describing Northside DART stations (including those serving this LEA) as comparatively 'neglected' versus Southside stations, reflecting ongoing local concern about station safety and anti-social behaviour. Separately, a serious domestic homicide was reported in Raheny in June 2023 (TheJournal.ie, Newstalk, 98fm) — a woman was found dead in a house and a man was later charged with her murder — but this was a domestic-violence case, not indicative of stranger or street danger to visitors or residents generally. Overall, daytime activity in the area shows no particular concern, while evening/night use of the DART stations along this stretch of line carries a documented, if localized and youth-related, pattern of anti-social behaviour and occasional violent incidents.

name: Kimmage-Rathmines
text: Press research found no evidence that Rathmines, Rathgar, Terenure or Harold's Cross are unusually dangerous, and daytime activity in the area shows no particular pattern of concern. The most concrete recent development is that An Garda Síochána extended high-visibility foot patrols to Rathmines, Rathgar and Terenure in April 2026 as part of the DMR South operation, a move Gardaí said was driven by community/business feedback and crime-location data (RTE, 23 April 2026); the wider operation's own statistics for the period show public-order and drunkenness offences up (consistent with pub/nightlife-heavy stretches like Rathmines), but theft from person down 33%, robbery from person down 33%, and serious assaults down 18% (The Irish Times, 23 April 2026) — suggesting nuisance/public-order issues rather than a worsening violent-crime trend. Documented incidents are sparse and mostly isolated: in February 2023 a man was jailed for two unprovoked 2021 knife attacks (Stanley blade) on fellow homeless men in Rathmines, one in church grounds and one near the canal, an incident tied to addiction/homelessness rather than random public danger (Irish Times); a July 2025 daytime robbery saw a man threaten a van owner with a crowbar after stealing tools from a Lower Rathmines Road car park (Garda Crimecall, September 2025); and Gardaí issued a witness appeal after a firearm was discharged in Kimmage in August 2023, with no further reporting found. Most notably, on 25-26 August 2026 (very recent, days before this report) the body of a woman in her 20s was found in Ravensdale Park, Kimmage — Gardaí stated the death was not being treated as suspicious at the time of reporting, though an investigation continued (RTE, Irish Times, TheJournal.ie, 28 August 2026). No pattern of muggings, gang activity, or no-go streets was found for this LEA; it remains a popular, generally safe residential and student area, with night ratings reflecting normal city nightlife/public-order caution rather than a specific danger pattern.

name: North Inner City
text: The North Inner City LEA — covering O'Connell Street, Parnell Square, Mountjoy Square, Sean McDermott Street, Sheriff Street, North Wall/docklands, Smithfield and the Connolly Station area — is one of Dublin's most heavily documented safety-concern districts, despite hosting major tourist attractions like the GPO and O'Connell Street itself. On the night of 23 November 2023, a knife attack that injured three children and a childcare worker near Parnell Square triggered a large-scale riot along O'Connell Street: Luas trams and Garda vehicles were burned, shops were looted, and Gardai clashed violently with a mob (Wikipedia's '2023 Dublin riot' entry; The Journal and Irish Times live coverage, 23 Nov 2023). More directly relevant to visitor safety, a Canadian tourist was assaulted on O'Connell Street on 23 June 2024 — kicked in the head with, per the trial judge, 'full force' — and died nine days later; two men were charged, and one was jailed for manslaughter in February 2026 (Irish Times, 2 July 2024 and 17 Feb 2026; TheJournal.ie; RTE, Feb 2026). Gardai separately logged a serious assault at Cathal Brugha Street/O'Connell Street on the same weekend in June 2024. Beyond individual incidents, open drug use and dealing are a persistent, officially acknowledged problem: in January 2024 the Irish Times reported a Dublin city-centre back street near O'Connell Street was closed to the public after the council said it could no longer control persistent drug use, antisocial behaviour and dumping there, and in July 2024 an Oireachtas committee heard the city centre was 'scourged with anti-social behaviour, drug-dealing, gang intimidation.' Newstalk has reported drug-related intimidation is 'a huge fact of life' for parts of the north inner city, particularly around Sean McDermott Street. Continuing coverage through 2025-2026 (TheJournal, Jan 2026; Dublin People, Aug 2026) shows the problem persisting despite a new Garda station on O'Connell Street and a Government-established Dublin City Taskforce with extra policing. Daytime, the area functions as a busy, heavily-trafficked tourist and shopping core with a visible Garda presence, so casual visits (GPO, Parnell Square cultural quarter, Smithfield) carry limited risk, but open drug dealing and street-level antisocial behaviour are visible even by day in patches. At night the combination of documented open drug scenes, gang intimidation, and at least one fatal, unprovoked tourist assault on the main thoroughfare itself justifies a red rating after dark, with a yellow rating during the day given the well-documented but more localized daytime issues.

name: Pembroke
text: The Pembroke Local Electoral Area, covering Ballsbridge, Donnybrook, Ranelagh, and Sandymount, is consistently described in Irish media and neighbourhood guides as one of Dublin's more affluent, low-crime districts, and a targeted search of Irish outlets (independent.ie, thejournal.ie, dublinlive.ie, rte.ie, herald.ie, irishmirror.ie, extra.ie) for the 2023-2026 period found little evidence of a recurring crime or anti-social-behaviour pattern in Ballsbridge, Donnybrook, or Sandymount specifically — searches for burglary, robbery, or assault reports tied to those neighbourhoods returned mostly generic real-estate or unrelated results, and general Dublin safety guides list these three areas among the city's safest. The one significant documented incident found was a serious and specific event in Ranelagh: on 2 September 2026, the Irish Times reported that four people were arrested and a man was hospitalised after a suspected knife attack at a shop in Ranelagh, described as a violent assault requiring Garda intervention. This appears to be an isolated, serious incident rather than part of an established pattern of violence in the area, and no comparable violent-crime reports were found for Ranelagh in the preceding years of coverage searched. No specific reports of daytime muggings, tourist-targeted theft, or chronic anti-social behaviour hotspots were found for any of the four neighbourhoods within Pembroke. Given the affluent, low-density, largely residential character of Ballsbridge, Donnybrook, and Sandymount, and the absence of any documented daytime safety concerns, daytime risk is assessed as low (green). The single serious, if isolated, violent incident in Ranelagh in September 2026 is enough to warrant a degree of caution after dark rather than a blanket 'no concern' rating, so night-time risk is assessed as yellow, reflecting an occasional but real capacity for serious incidents even in an otherwise low-crime area, rather than any entrenched pattern.
sources: GetMyHomeReport Dublin Crime Statistics by Area (getmyhomereport.ie)

name: South East Inner City
text: This LEA covers Dublin's densest tourist core — Temple Bar, Grafton Street, Trinity College and St Stephen's Green — and press coverage from 2024-2026 shows a marked gap between daytime and nighttime risk. By day, the main documented issue is petty and organised theft: Newstalk and Garda press material describe pickpocket gangs (including an 'Oliver Twist'-style operation that led to roughly 40 arrests in an undercover crackdown) specifically working Dublin city-centre tourist hotspots such as Grafton Street and Temple Bar, a long-running pattern rather than a single incident. There have also been isolated daytime/evening assaults reported near St Stephen's Green, including a Garda witness appeal after a man in his 30s was hospitalised following an assault at St Stephen's Green West on the August bank holiday Monday in 2024 (TheJournal.ie, Garda.ie). At night, however, the picture is significantly more serious. In February 2026, a man was critically injured in a violent assault in Temple Bar; two men were arrested and later charged with a 'vicious' attack, and after the victim — identified as an English tourist — died of his injuries, one of the accused was charged with murder (RTÉ, Irish Times, BreakingNews.ie, 19-27 Feb 2026). Separately, in June 2026, 21-year-old Qayyum Balogun was fatally stabbed just off Grafton Street near Clarendon Street after being chased by a large group following a row near a venue hosting a concert at Bewley's; a bystander was also stabbed in the same incident, and multiple arrests and charges followed, including of a man accused of leading a '14-man pack' that chased the victim (TheJournal.ie, RTÉ, Irish Times, June 2026). These two fatal or near-fatal nighttime attacks within months of each other, both tied to late-night/nightlife circumstances in the heart of the tourist district, represent a well-documented and serious pattern rather than an isolated event, distinct from the area's long-standing but comparatively minor daytime pickpocketing problem. No pattern of daytime muggings or serious daytime violence specifically was found beyond the theft and the isolated Stephen's Green assault, so daytime risk is rated as limited/localized (yellow) while nighttime risk, given the two 2026 homicide-related cases centred on Temple Bar and Grafton Street, is rated red.

name: South West Inner City
text: The South West Inner City LEA (Dublin 8's Liberties, Kilmainham, Rialto, Dolphin's Barn and surrounds) is a genuinely split area: its tourist core (Guinness Storehouse, Christ Church Cathedral, Kilmainham Gaol) draws no notable recent negative press, but the residential streets around and behind these sites carry some of Dublin's most persistently documented deprivation and drug-related problems. An April 2026 Trinity College Dublin report by economist Barra Roantree, covered by the Irish Times, found the wider south-west inner city area (Dublin 8, including the Liberties, Rialto, Dolphin's Barn, Kilmainham, Inchicore and Islandbridge, population c.45,000) has a crime rate of 106.7 per 1,000 residents versus a 40.4 national average — more than double — plus drug-poisoning deaths roughly double the national rate (22 in 2021) and annual crime-related costs estimated at €60 million, prompting the appointment of a dedicated Dublin regeneration "tsar." At street level, the Oliver Bond flats complex on Bridgefoot Street, squarely in the Liberties, has been repeatedly documented: TheJournal.ie (March 2021) quoted residents describing "astronomical" crack cocaine and heroin sales and living "in fear," and The Liberty (March 2023) reported daylight open drug use, discarded needles in common areas, children as young as five exposed to dealing, and minors allegedly recruited into the trade — a pattern the Irish Times (March 2024) also linked historically to organised crime networks. Fatima Mansions, further south near Rialto, was historically dubbed the "heroin supermarket" by the Irish Times, though no specific 2023-2026 coverage of ongoing problems there was found, suggesting past regeneration efforts have had some effect and current claims about that specific spot should not be overstated. Separately, tourists were robbed at gunpoint near the Guinness Storehouse in October 2019 (widely covered by the Irish Times, Irish Examiner and Irish Post) — a serious but now dated incident with no comparable repeat found in the 2023-2026 window. Overall: the marquee tourist attractions themselves show no particular daytime concern, but the surrounding LEA has real, repeated, well-documented open drug-dealing hotspots and crime rates far above the national average, which combined with generally reduced footfall and visibility after dark, tips the night rating toward red while day stays at a more cautious yellow.
